Angle:

The angle is defined as the amount of revolution that the revolving line makes with its initial position.

Generally the angle is taken positive if it is traced by the revolving line in anticlockwise direction. The angle is taken negative if it is covered in clockwise direction.

1° = 60' (minute)

1' = 60" (second)

Relation between Angle and Arc

$\text { Angle }(\theta)=\dfrac{\text { Arc }}{\text { Radius }}=\dfrac{\ell}{\mathrm{r}}$

To convert an angle from degree to radian multiply it by $\dfrac{\pi}{180^{\circ}}$

To convert an angle from radian to degree multiply it by $\dfrac{180^{\circ}}{\pi}$

Trigonometric Ratios (or T ratios)

$\sin \theta=\dfrac{\mathrm{P}}{\mathrm{H}} \quad \operatorname{cosec} \theta=\dfrac{\mathrm{H}}{\mathrm{P}} \quad \cos \theta=\dfrac{\mathrm{B}}{\mathrm{H}} \quad \sec \theta=\dfrac{\mathrm{H}}{\mathrm{~B}} \quad \tan \theta=\dfrac{\mathrm{P}}{\mathrm{~B}} \quad \cot \theta=\dfrac{\mathrm{B}}{\mathrm{P}}$

$\operatorname{cosec} \theta=\dfrac{1}{\sin \theta} \quad \sec \theta=\dfrac{1}{\cos \theta} \quad \cot \theta=\dfrac{1}{\tan \theta}$

Trigonometric Identities

$\begin{aligned} & \sin ^2 \theta+\cos ^2 \theta=1 \\ & 1+\tan ^2 \theta=\sec ^2 \theta \\ & 1+\cot ^2 \theta=\operatorname{cosec}^2 \theta \end{aligned}$

Quadrants & ASTC Rule :

In first quadrant, all trigonometric ratios are positive.

In second quadrant, only sin$\theta$ and cosec $\theta$ are positive.

In third quadrant, only tan$\theta$ and cot $\theta$ are positive.

In fourth quadrant, only cos$\theta$ and sec $\theta$ are positive

Trigonometrical Ratios of General Angles (Reduction Formulae)

(1)    Trigonometric function of an angle $(2 \mathrm{n} \pi+\theta)$ where n = 0, 1, 2, 3,.... will be remain same.

$\sin (2 n \pi+\theta)=\sin \theta \quad \\[10 pt] \cos (2 n \pi+\theta)=\cos \theta \quad \\[10 pt] \tan (2 n \pi+\theta)=\tan \theta$

(2) Trigonometric function of an angle $\left(\frac{\mathrm{n} \pi}{2}+\theta\right)$  will remain same if n is even and sign of trigonometric function will be according to value of that function in quadrant.

$\sin (\pi-\theta)=+\sin \theta \\[10 pt]  \cos (\pi-\theta)=-\cos \theta  \\[10 pt]  \tan (\pi-\theta)=-\tan \theta$

$ \sin (\pi+\theta)=-\sin \theta \\[10 pt]  \cos (\pi+\theta)=-\cos \theta \\[10 pt] \tan (\pi+\theta)=+\tan \theta$

$ \sin (2 \pi-\theta)=-\sin \theta  \\[10 pt] \cos (2 \pi-\theta)=+\cos \theta  \\[10 pt]  \tan (2 \pi-\theta)=-\tan \theta $

(3) Trigonometric function of an angle$\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{n} \pi}{2}+\theta\right)$ will be changed into co-function if n is odd and sign of trigonometric function will be according to value of that function in quadrant.

$\displaystyle \sin \left(\frac{\pi}{2}+\theta\right)=+\cos \theta \\[10 pt]  \cos \left(\frac{\pi}{2}+\theta\right)=-\sin \theta \\[10 pt]  \tan \left(\frac{\pi}{2}+\theta\right)=-\cot \theta$

$\displaystyle \sin \left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)=+\cos \theta  \\[10 pt]  \cos \left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)=+\sin \theta \\[10 pt] \tan \left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)=+\cot \theta $

(4) Trigonometric function of an angle –$\theta$ (negative angles)

$\sin (-\theta)=-\sin \theta \quad \\[10 pt] \cos (-\theta)=+\cos \theta \quad \\[10 pt] \tan (-\theta)=-\tan \theta$

Sum property for sine function

sin(A + B) = sinAcosB + cosAsinB

sin(A – B) = sinA cosB – cosAsinB

Sum property for cosine function

cos(A + B) = cosAcosB – sinAsinB

cos(A – B) = cosAcosB + sinAsinB

Sum property for tan function

$\begin{aligned} & \tan (A+B)=\frac{\tan A+\tan B}{1-\tan A \tan B} \\[10 pt] & \tan (A-B)=\frac{\tan A-\tan B}{1+\tan A \tan B} \end{aligned}$

Double angle property

$\begin{aligned} & \sin 2 \mathrm{~A}=2 \sin \mathrm{~A} \cos \mathrm{~A} \\ & \cos 2 \mathrm{~A}=\cos ^2 \mathrm{~A}-\sin ^2 \mathrm{~A} \\ & \tan 2 \mathrm{~A}=\frac{2 \tan \mathrm{~A}}{1-\tan ^2 \mathrm{~A}} \end{aligned}$

Range of Trigonometric Functions

$\begin{array}{lll} \sin \theta=\dfrac{\mathrm{P}}{\mathrm{H}} & \longrightarrow & -1 \leq \sin \theta \leq 1 \\[10 pt] \cos \theta=\dfrac{\mathrm{B}}{\mathrm{H}} & \longrightarrow & -1 \leq \cos \theta \leq 1 \\[10 pt] \tan \theta=\dfrac{\mathrm{P}}{\mathrm{~B}} & \longrightarrow & -\infty<\tan \theta<+\infty \end{array}$

T-Ratios of Special Angles

$\sin \theta=\dfrac{3}{5} ; \quad \cos \theta=\dfrac{4}{5} ; \quad \tan \theta=\dfrac{3}{4}$

$\sin \theta=\dfrac{4}{5} ; \quad \cos \theta=\dfrac{3}{5} ; \quad \tan \theta=\dfrac{4}{3}$

Definition of Differentiation/Derivative

$\frac{d y}{d x}$ = "instantaneous rate of change of  y w.r.t $x$"

The ratio of small change in the function y and the variable x is called the instantaneous rate of change of y w.r.t. x.

Differentiation Formula

1.$\frac{d}{d x}\left(x^n\right)=n \cdot x^{n-1}$

2.$\frac{d}{d x}[c]=0$

3.$\frac{d}{d x}\left(e^x\right)=e^x$

4.$\frac{d}{d x}\left(a^x\right)=a^x \ln (a)$

5.$\frac{d}{d x}(\ln (x))=\frac{1}{x}$

6.$\frac{d}{d x}\left(\log _a(x)\right)=\frac{1}{x \ln (a)}$

7.$\frac{d}{d x}(\sin x)=\cos x$

8.$\frac{d}{d x}(\cos x)=-\sin x$

9.$\frac{d}{d x}(\tan x)=\sec ^2 x$

10.$\frac{d}{d x}(\cot x)=-\cosec ^2 x$

11.$\frac{d}{d x}(\sec x)=\sec x \tan x$

12.$\frac{d}{d x}(\cosec x)=-\cosec x \cot x$

Constant Multiple Rule

$\text { If } y=c f(x)=c U \text {, then }: \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{d(c U)}{d x}=c \frac{d U}{d x}$

Addition/Subtraction Rule

If U and V are functions of x and y is sum of functions U and V :

$y=U \pm V, \frac{d(U \pm V)}{d x}=\frac{d U}{d x} \pm \frac{d V}{d x}$

Product Rule

$\frac{d(U V)}{d x}=V \frac{d U}{d x}+U \frac{d V}{d x}$

Quotient Rule

$\frac{d\left(\frac{U}{V}\right)}{d x}=\frac{V \frac{d U}{d x}-U \frac{d V}{d x}}{V^2}$

Rules of Differentiation - Chain Rule

If $y = f(U)$

$\displaystyle \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{d f(U)}{d U} \times \frac{d U}{d x} ,$

Power Chain Rule

$\text { If } y=U^n \text { then } \frac{d y}{d x} \text { will be given by : }$

$\frac{d y}{d x}=n U^{(n-1)} \frac{d U}{d x}$

Application of Derivatives

Slope of a curve at a given point

$\mathrm{m}_{\text {inst }}=\tan \theta=\frac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{dx}}$

Function to First Derivative:

$y = f(x) \quad \xrightarrow{\text{Differentiation}} \quad \frac{dy}{dx}$

First Derivative to Second Derivative :

$\frac{dy}{dx} \quad \xrightarrow{\text{Differentiation}} \quad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$

Maxima

Condition for maxima are :

$\frac{d y}{d x}=0 \text { and } \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}<0$

Minima

Condition for minima are:

$\frac{d y}{d x}=0 \text { and } \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}>0$

$\text { Slope of the tangent at } x=0, \frac{d y}{d x}=2(0)+2=2$

$\text { Slope of the tangent at } x=-1, \frac{d y}{d x}=2(-1)+2=0$

Integration:

$\int \mathrm{f}(\mathrm{x}) \mathrm{dx}=\mathrm{F}(\mathrm{x})+\mathrm{c}$

Formulae of Integration for Algebraic function

1.$\int x^n d x=\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}+c$

2.$\int \frac{1}{x} d x=\ln x+c$

3.$\int \mathrm{kdx}=\mathrm{kx}+\mathrm{c}$

4.$\int \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{x}} \mathrm{dx}=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{x}}+\mathrm{c}$

5.$\int \sin x d x=-\cos x+c$

6.$\int \cos x d x=\sin x+c$

Definite Integration :

When a function is integrated between a lower limit and an upper limit, it is called a definite integral.

$\int_{\mathrm{a}}^{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{f}(\mathrm{x}) \mathrm{dx}=[\mathrm{F}(\mathrm{x})]_{\mathrm{a}}^{\mathrm{b}}=[\mathrm{F}(\mathrm{~b})-\mathrm{F}(\mathrm{a})]$

Average Value of Function

$<y>=\frac{\int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{\mathrm{x}_2} \mathrm{f}(\mathrm{x}) \mathrm{dx}}{\int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{\mathrm{x}_2} \mathrm{dx}}$

$<\mathrm{y}>=\frac{\text { area under } \mathrm{y}-\mathrm{x} \text { curve }}{\text { range of } \mathrm{x}(\mathrm{~b}-\mathrm{a})}$

Area under a curve and definite integration

$\int_a^b f(x) d x=\text { shaded area between curve and } x \text {-axis. }$

$\int_{\mathrm{a}}^{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{f}(\mathrm{x}) \mathrm{dx}=[\mathrm{F}(\mathrm{x})]_{\mathrm{a}}^{\mathrm{b}}=[\mathrm{F}(\mathrm{~b})-\mathrm{F}(\mathrm{a})]$

Applications of Integration – Analytical

There are many applications of integration such as :

(a) Displacement/Change in position  $\Delta \mathrm{x}=\mathrm{x}_2-\mathrm{x}_1$

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{v}=\frac{\mathrm{dx}}{\mathrm{dt}} \\ & \int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{\mathrm{x}_2} \mathrm{dx}=\int_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{\mathrm{t}_2} \mathrm{vdt} \end{aligned}$

$\text { (Change in position) } \quad \mathrm{x}_2-\mathrm{x}_1=\int_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{\mathrm{t}_2} \mathrm{vdt}$

(b) Change in velocity  $\Delta v=v_2-v_1$

$a=\frac{d v}{d t}$

$\int_{\mathrm{v}_1}^{\mathrm{v}_2} \mathrm{~d} v=\int_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{\mathrm{t}_2} \mathrm{adt}$

$\text { (Change in velocity) } \quad \mathrm{v}_2-\mathrm{v}_1=\int_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{\mathrm{t}_2} \text { adt }$

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: Find average value of a function $\mathrm{I}=\mathrm{I}_0 \cos \mathrm{t}$ in interval of time $\left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$
blocks.answer:
Answer  $\dfrac{2 \mathrm{I}_0}{\pi} \text { unit }$

$\langle\mathrm{I}\rangle=\frac{\int_0^{\pi / 2}\left(I_0 \cos t\right) d t}{\frac{\pi}{2}-0}$

$=\frac{\mathrm{I}_0 \int_0^{\pi / 2} \cos t \mathrm{dt}}{\frac{\pi}{2}}$

$= \frac{I_0[\sin t]_0^{\pi / 2}}{\pi / 2}$

$=\frac{\mathrm{I}_0}{\frac{\pi}{2}}=\frac{2 \mathrm{I}_0}{\pi} \text { unit }$

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question: Find area under the curve $y=2 x^2-4 x+6$ from x = 2 to x = 4.
blocks.answer:
Answer  $\dfrac{76}{3} \text { unit }$

$\text { Area under the curve }=\int_{x_1}^{x_2} y d x=\int_2^4\left(2 x^2-4 x+6\right) d x=$

$\int_2^4 2 x^2 d x-\int_2^4 4 x d x+\int_2^4 6 d x$

$=\left[\frac{2 x^3}{3}\right]_2^4-\left[2 x^2\right]_2^4+[6 x]_2^4=\left(\frac{112}{3}\right)-(24)+12=\frac{76}{3} \text { unit }$

Quadratic Equation: An algebraic equation of second order (Highest power of the variable is equal to 2) is called a quadratic equation.

$a x^2+b x+c=0$

$\text { where } a \neq 0$

The general solution of the quadratic equation

$\mathrm{x}=\frac{-\mathrm{b} \pm \sqrt{\mathrm{D}}}{2 \mathrm{a}}$ , $\text { where } D=b^2-4 a c$

Condition for Real and Imaginary Roots

$\begin{aligned} &\text { For Real Roots }\\ &\begin{aligned} & D \geq 0 \\ & b^2-4 a c \geq 0 \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} &\text { For Imaginary Roots }\\ &\begin{aligned} & D<0 \\ & b^2-4 a c<0 \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$

Sum and Product of Roots

$\begin{aligned} &\text { Sum of the roots }\\ &\mathrm{x}_1+\mathrm{x}_2=-\frac{\mathrm{b}}{\mathrm{a}} \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} &\text { Product of the roots }\\ &\mathrm{x}_1 \mathrm{x}_2=\frac{\mathrm{c}}{\mathrm{a}} \end{aligned}$

Binomial Theorem: An algebraic expression containing two terms is called a binomial expression

$(1+x)^n=1+n x+\frac{n(n-1)}{2 \times 1} x^2+\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{3 \times 2 \times 1} x^2+\ldots \ldots$

Arithmetic Progression (AP)

General form: a, (a + d), (a + 2d), ……., [a + (n – 1) d]

Here First Term : a

Common Difference : d

$\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{th}} \text { Term : } \quad[\mathrm{a}+(\mathrm{n}-1) \mathrm{d}]$

$\begin{aligned} &\text { Sum of first } \mathrm{n} \text { terms: }\\ &\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{n}}=\frac{\mathrm{n}}{2}\left[1^{\text {st }} \text { term }+\mathrm{n}^{\text {th }} \text { term }\right] \Rightarrow \mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{n}}=\frac{\mathrm{n}}{2}[2 \mathrm{a}+(\mathrm{n}-1) \mathrm{d}] \end{aligned}$

Geometric Progression (GP)

$\text { a, ar, } \operatorname{ar}^2, \ldots \ldots \ldots \ldots \ldots \operatorname{ar}^{(n-1)}$

First Term : a

Common Ratio : r

$\mathrm{n}^{\text {th }} \text { Term: }$$\mathrm{ar}^{(\mathrm{n}-1)}$

$\begin{aligned} &\text { Sum of first } \mathrm{n} \text { terms : }\\ &S_n=\frac{a\left(1-r^n\right)}{(1-r)} \end{aligned}$

Sum of all the terms of an infinite GP $S_{\infty}=\frac{a}{(1-r)} ; \text { Only when }|r|<1 $

Formulae to Remember

$1+2+3+4+5+\ldots \ldots+n=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$

$1^2+2^2+3^2+4^2+5^2+\ldots \ldots+n^2=\frac{n(n+1)(2 n+1)}{6}$

$1^3+2^3+3^3+4^3+5^3+\ldots \ldots+n^3=\left(\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\right)^2$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Physical Quantities: Those physical quantities which are used to define law of physics is known as physical quantities.

On the basis of directions, there are mainly two types of physical quantities.

(1) Scalar Quantities: A physical quantity which can be described completely by its magnitude only and does not require a direction is known as a scalar quantity. Ex: Distance, mass, time, speed

(2) Vector Quantities: A physical quantity which requires magnitude and a particular direction, when it is expressed.

(a) has a specified direction.

(b) obeys law of vector addition, then only it is said to be a vector.

Representation of vector:

Parallel vectors : Those vectors which have same direction are called parallel vectors. Angle between two parallel vectors is always 0°

Equal Vectors : Vectors which have equal magnitude and same direction are called equal vectors.

Anti–parallel Vectors : Those vectors which have opposite direction are called anti–parallel vector. Angle between two anti–parallel vectors is always 180°.

Co-initial vector : Co-initial vectors are those vectors which have the same initial point.

Collinear Vectors : The vectors lying in the same line are known as collinear vectors. Angle between collinear vectors is either 0° or 180°.

Coplanar Vectors : Vectors located in the same plane are called coplanar vectors.

Unit Vector : A vector having unit magnitude is called unit vector. It is used to specify direction. A unit vector is represented by

$\hat{A}=\frac{\vec{A}}{|\vec{A}|}$ $\left(\text { unit vector }=\frac{\text { Vector }}{\text { Magnitude of the vector }}\right)$

Note:

  • Axial Vectors: These vectors are used in rotational motion to define rotational effects.
  • A vector can be broken down into its components along the coordinate axes (typically the x, y, and z axes).
  • A unit vector is a vector with a magnitude of 1.It indicates direction but has no specific magnitude.

Addition of  vectors

1.Triangle law of addition of two vectors: If two vectors are represented by two sides of a triangle in same order then their sum or 'resultant vector' is given by the third side of the triangle taken in opposite order of the first two vectors.

$\vec{R} = \vec{A} + \vec{B}$

2. Parallelogram Law:  If two vectors are represented by two adjacent sides of a parallelogram which are directed away from their common point then their sum (i.e. resultant vector) is given by the diagonal of the parallelogram passing away through that common point.

$\overrightarrow{PQ} + \overrightarrow{PS} = \overrightarrow{PR}$

$\vec{R} = \vec{A} + \vec{B}$

Analytical Method

$|\mathbf{R}| = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + 2AB \cos \theta}$

$|\vec{A} + \vec{B}| = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + 2AB \cos \theta}$

$In~ ΔOPQ$

$\tan \alpha = \frac{QP}{OQ}$=$\frac{B \sin \theta}{A + B \cos \theta}$

$\tan \beta = \frac{A \sin \theta}{B + A \cos \theta}$

Special Cases:

(1) If two vectors are parallel : $\theta = 0^\circ$

$|\vec{R}|_{\text{max}} = A + B$

(2) If two vectors are anti-parallel: $\theta =180^\circ$

$|\vec{R}|_{\text{min}} = A - B$

(3) If two vectors are perpendicular: $\theta = 90^\circ$

$|\vec{R}| = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2}$

$\vec{R} = \left| \vec{A} + \vec{B} \right| = 2A \cos \left( \frac{\theta}{2} \right)$

Note: $A - B \leq |\vec{A} + \vec{B}| \leq A + B$

Properties of vector addition:

1. Vector addition is commutative :$\vec{A} + \vec{B} = \vec{B} + \vec{A}$

2.Vector addition is associative:  $\left( {\vec A + \vec B} \right) + \vec C = \left( {\vec B + \vec C} \right) + \vec A = \left( {\vec C + \vec A} \right) + \vec B$

3.If two vectors  $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}}
$ & $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{~B}}$ are of equal magnitude ,i.e $|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}}|=|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}|=\mathrm{a}$.

Then the magnitude of their vector addition: $\left| {\vec R} \right| = \left| {\vec A + \vec B} \right| = 2a\cos \left( {\frac{\theta }{2}} \right)$

Addition of more than two vectors (law of polygon): If some vectors are represented by sides of a polygon in same order, then their resultant vector is represented by the closing side of polygon in the opposite order.

$\vec{R} = \vec{A} + \vec{B} + \vec{C} + \vec{D}$

If n coplanar vectors of equal magnitude are at equal angular separation $(\frac{360^\circ}{n})$ then their resultant is always ZERO.

Subtraction of two vectors :

Let $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are two vectors. Their difference  $\vec{A} - \vec{B}$ can be treated as sum of the vector $\vec{A}$ and $({- \overrightarrow{B}})$.

$\vec{A} - \vec{B} = \vec{A} + (-\vec{B})$

$|\vec{A} - \vec{B}| = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 - 2AB \cos \theta}$

$\tan \alpha = \frac{B \sin \theta}{A - B \cos \theta}$

Properties of vector subtraction :

1.Vector subtraction does not follow commutative law

$\vec{A} - \vec{B} \neq \vec{B} - \vec{A}$

2.Vector subtraction does not follow associative law

$(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}}-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}})-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{C}} \neq (\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{C}})-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}}\neq (\overrightarrow{\mathrm{C}}-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}})-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}$

3.If two vectors are of  equal magnitude i.e $|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}}|=|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}|=\mathrm{a}$ then magnitude of their vector subtraction

$|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{s}}|=$$\left| \vec{A} - \vec{B} \right| = 2a \sin \left( \frac{\theta}{2} \right)$

Resolution of Vectors: To break or split a vector in components is called resolution of vector. Any vector can be split in two or more than two components.

Note: Maximum number of components of a vector can be infinite.

Vector Resolution in A Plane (2D): If the angle between components is 90°, then they are known as perpendicular/orthogonal /rectangular components.

$A_x = \text{Component of } \vec{A} \text{ along the x-axis}$

$A_y = \text{Component of } \vec{A} \text{ along the y-axis}$

$A_x = A \cos \theta$

$A_y = A \sin \theta$

$\vec{A} = A_x \hat{i} + A_y \hat{j}$

$\vec{A} = A \cos \theta \, \hat{i} + A \sin \theta \, \hat{j}$

$|\vec{A}| = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2}$

$\tan \theta = \frac{A_y}{A_x}$

$\tan \phi = \frac{A_x}{A_y}$

Here  $\theta$ is angle between $\vec{A}$ and its x component Here $\phi$ is angle between $\vec{A}$ and its y component

Resolution of vectors in 3-D

If  $\vec{A}$ makes angle $\alpha$ with x- axis angle $\beta$with y- axis angle $\gamma$ with z- axis.

Component of $\vec{A}$ along x axis is $\mathbf{A}_{\mathbf{x}}$

Component of $\vec{A}$ along y- axis is $\mathbf{A}_{\mathbf{y}}$

Component of $\vec{A}$ along z- axis is $\mathbf{A}_{\mathbf{z}}$

$\cos \alpha=\frac{A_x}{A} \Rightarrow A_x=A \cos \alpha \quad ; \cos \beta=\frac{A_y}{A} \Rightarrow A_y=A \cos \beta \quad ; \cos \gamma=\frac{A_z}{A} \Rightarrow A_z=A \cos \gamma$$$

Here, $cos \alpha$, $\cos \beta$ and  $\cos \gamma$ are known as direction cosines of  $\vec{A}$

$\text { As, } A_x, A_y \text { and } A_z \text { are components of } \vec{A} $

$\vec{A}=A_x \hat{\imath}+A_y \hat{\jmath}+A_z \hat{k} \Rightarrow A=\sqrt{A_x^2+A_y^2+A_z^2}$

$\sin ^2 \alpha+\sin ^2 \beta+\sin ^2 \gamma=2$

$\cos ^2 \alpha+\cos ^2 \beta+\cos ^2 \gamma=1$

$\vec{A}=A_x \hat{\imath}+A_y \hat{\jmath}+A_z \hat{k} \Rightarrow \frac{\vec{A}}{A}=\frac{A_x}{A} \hat{\imath}+\frac{A_y}{A} \hat{\jmath}+\frac{A_z}{A} \hat{k} \Rightarrow \widehat{A}=\cos \alpha \hat{\imath}+\cos \beta \hat{\jmath}+\cos \gamma \hat{k}$

Multiplication of a Vector by Scalar:

1. Whenever a vector is multiplied by a positive number then the new vector has same direction but its magnitude changes depending on number.

2. Whenever a vector is multiplied by a negative number then the new vector has opposite direction and its magnitude changes depending on number.

Scalar Product: The scalar product of two vectors $\vec{A}$ and$\vec{B}$ equals to the product of their magnitudes and the cosine of the angle $\theta$ between them.

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~B}}=|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}}||\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}| \cos \theta$

Range of dot product: $-{A B} \leq \overrightarrow{{A}} \cdot \overrightarrow{{B}} \leq {A B}$

Notes:

• Dot product of two perpendicular vectors is always zero

• If the dot product of two non-zero vectors is zero, then $\theta=90^{\circ}$

$\begin{aligned} & \vec{A} \cdot \vec{A}=A^2 \\ & \widehat{A} \cdot \widehat{A}=1 \end{aligned}$

$\hat{\mathrm{i}} \cdot \hat{\mathrm{i}}=\hat{\mathrm{j}} \cdot \hat{\mathrm{j}}=\hat{\mathrm{k}} \cdot \hat{\mathrm{k}}=1$

Vector product :The vector product or cross product of any two vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ denoted as $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}(\mathrm{read} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~A}} \text { cross } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}})$ is defined as  $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}=\mathrm{AB} \sin \theta \hat{\mathrm{n}}$

Here $\theta$ is the angle between the vectors and the direction  is given by the right-hand-thumb rule($\overrightarrow{\mathrm{n}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}$)

  • Vector product of two vectors is always a vector perpendicular to the plane containing the two vectors, i.e. orthogonal (perpendicular) to both the vectors $\vec{A}$ and  $\vec{B}$
• Vector product of two vectors is not commutative

Application of Cross Product

1. To Find Area of Geometrical Shape

a. $\text { Area of Triangle }=\frac{1}{2}|\vec{A} \times \vec{B}|$

b. Area of Parallelogram

$\text { Area of parallelogram }=|\vec{A} \times \vec{B}| \quad $

Case II: If $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$  are diagonals of parallelogram

$\text { Area of parallelogram }=\frac{1}{2}|\vec{A} \times \vec{B}|$

2.To Find Unit vector perpendicular to given plane

$\hat{\mathrm{n}}= \pm \frac{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}}{|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{~A}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}|}= \pm \frac{\widehat{\mathrm{A}} \times \widehat{\mathrm{B}}}{\sin \theta}$

3. To Check Coplanarity

$\text { If } \vec{A}, \vec{B} ~\& ~ \vec{C} \text { are three coplanar vectors then }\\ (\vec{A} \times \vec{B}) \cdot \vec{C}=0 \Rightarrow[\vec{A}, \vec{B}, \vec{C}]=0$

blocks.answer: $\begin{aligned} &\text { Condition of coplanarity : }(\vec{A} \times \vec{B}) \cdot \vec{C}=0\\ &|\vec{A} \times \vec{B}|=\left|\begin{array}{ccc} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \end{array}\right|=\hat{i}(1-0)-\hat{j}(2-0)+\hat{k}(4-1)=\hat{i}-2 \hat{j}+3 \hat{k} \end{aligned}$$\begin{aligned} &\text { Using the condition of coplanarity : }(\vec{A} \times \vec{B}) \cdot \vec{C}=0\\ &=(\hat{i}-2 \hat{j}+3 \hat{k}) \cdot(3 \hat{i}-\hat{j}+x \hat{k})=0 \Rightarrow 3+2+3 x=0 \Rightarrow-5=3 x \Rightarrow x=-\frac{5}{3} \end{aligned}$

blocks.text:
Angle:

The angle is defined as the amount of revolution that the revolving line makes with its initial position.

Generally the angle is taken positive if it is traced by the revolving line in anticlockwise direction. The angle is taken negative if it is covered in clockwise direction.

1° = 60' (minute)

1' = 60" (second)

Relation between Angle and Arc

$\text { Angle }(\theta)=\dfrac{\text { Arc }}{\text { Radius }}=\dfrac{\ell}{\mathrm{r}}$

To convert an angle from degree to radian multiply it by $\dfrac{\pi}{180^{\circ}}$

To convert an angle from radian to degree multiply it by $\dfrac{180^{\circ}}{\pi}$

Trigonometric Ratios (or T ratios)

$\sin \theta=\dfrac{\mathrm{P}}{\mathrm{H}} \quad \operatorname{cosec} \theta=\dfrac{\mathrm{H}}{\mathrm{P}} \quad \cos \theta=\dfrac{\mathrm{B}}{\mathrm{H}} \quad \sec \theta=\dfrac{\mathrm{H}}{\mathrm{~B}} \quad \tan \theta=\dfrac{\mathrm{P}}{\mathrm{~B}} \quad \cot \theta=\dfrac{\mathrm{B}}{\mathrm{P}}$

$\operatorname{cosec} \theta=\dfrac{1}{\sin \theta} \quad \sec \theta=\dfrac{1}{\cos \theta} \quad \cot \theta=\dfrac{1}{\tan \theta}$

Trigonometric Identities

$\begin{aligned} & \sin ^2 \theta+\cos ^2 \theta=1 \\ & 1+\tan ^2 \theta=\sec ^2 \theta \\ & 1+\cot ^2 \theta=\operatorname{cosec}^2 \theta \end{aligned}$

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Quadrants & ASTC Rule :

In first quadrant, all trigonometric ratios are positive.

In second quadrant, only sin$\theta$ and cosec $\theta$ are positive.

In third quadrant, only tan$\theta$ and cot $\theta$ are positive.

In fourth quadrant, only cos$\theta$ and sec $\theta$ are positive

Trigonometrical Ratios of General Angles (Reduction Formulae)

(1)    Trigonometric function of an angle $(2 \mathrm{n} \pi+\theta)$ where n = 0, 1, 2, 3,.... will be remain same.

$\sin (2 n \pi+\theta)=\sin \theta \quad \\[10 pt] \cos (2 n \pi+\theta)=\cos \theta \quad \\[10 pt] \tan (2 n \pi+\theta)=\tan \theta$

(2) Trigonometric function of an angle $\left(\frac{\mathrm{n} \pi}{2}+\theta\right)$  will remain same if n is even and sign of trigonometric function will be according to value of that function in quadrant.

$\sin (\pi-\theta)=+\sin \theta \\[10 pt]  \cos (\pi-\theta)=-\cos \theta  \\[10 pt]  \tan (\pi-\theta)=-\tan \theta$

$ \sin (\pi+\theta)=-\sin \theta \\[10 pt]  \cos (\pi+\theta)=-\cos \theta \\[10 pt] \tan (\pi+\theta)=+\tan \theta$

$ \sin (2 \pi-\theta)=-\sin \theta  \\[10 pt] \cos (2 \pi-\theta)=+\cos \theta  \\[10 pt]  \tan (2 \pi-\theta)=-\tan \theta $

(3) Trigonometric function of an angle$\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{n} \pi}{2}+\theta\right)$ will be changed into co-function if n is odd and sign of trigonometric function will be according to value of that function in quadrant.

$\displaystyle \sin \left(\frac{\pi}{2}+\theta\right)=+\cos \theta \\[10 pt]  \cos \left(\frac{\pi}{2}+\theta\right)=-\sin \theta \\[10 pt]  \tan \left(\frac{\pi}{2}+\theta\right)=-\cot \theta$

$\displaystyle \sin \left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)=+\cos \theta  \\[10 pt]  \cos \left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)=+\sin \theta \\[10 pt] \tan \left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)=+\cot \theta $

(4) Trigonometric function of an angle –$\theta$ (negative angles)

$\sin (-\theta)=-\sin \theta \quad \\[10 pt] \cos (-\theta)=+\cos \theta \quad \\[10 pt] \tan (-\theta)=-\tan \theta$

Sum property for sine function

sin(A + B) = sinAcosB + cosAsinB

sin(A – B) = sinA cosB – cosAsinB

Sum property for cosine function

cos(A + B) = cosAcosB – sinAsinB

cos(A – B) = cosAcosB + sinAsinB

Sum property for tan function

$\begin{aligned} & \tan (A+B)=\frac{\tan A+\tan B}{1-\tan A \tan B} \\[10 pt] & \tan (A-B)=\frac{\tan A-\tan B}{1+\tan A \tan B} \end{aligned}$

Double angle property

$\begin{aligned} & \sin 2 \mathrm{~A}=2 \sin \mathrm{~A} \cos \mathrm{~A} \\ & \cos 2 \mathrm{~A}=\cos ^2 \mathrm{~A}-\sin ^2 \mathrm{~A} \\ & \tan 2 \mathrm{~A}=\frac{2 \tan \mathrm{~A}}{1-\tan ^2 \mathrm{~A}} \end{aligned}$

Range of Trigonometric Functions

$\begin{array}{lll} \sin \theta=\dfrac{\mathrm{P}}{\mathrm{H}} & \longrightarrow & -1 \leq \sin \theta \leq 1 \\[10 pt] \cos \theta=\dfrac{\mathrm{B}}{\mathrm{H}} & \longrightarrow & -1 \leq \cos \theta \leq 1 \\[10 pt] \tan \theta=\dfrac{\mathrm{P}}{\mathrm{~B}} & \longrightarrow & -\infty<\tan \theta<+\infty \end{array}$

T-Ratios of Special Angles

$\sin \theta=\dfrac{3}{5} ; \quad \cos \theta=\dfrac{4}{5} ; \quad \tan \theta=\dfrac{3}{4}$

$\sin \theta=\dfrac{4}{5} ; \quad \cos \theta=\dfrac{3}{5} ; \quad \tan \theta=\dfrac{4}{3}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Definition of Differentiation/Derivative

$\frac{d y}{d x}$ = "instantaneous rate of change of  y w.r.t $x$"

The ratio of small change in the function y and the variable x is called the instantaneous rate of change of y w.r.t. x.

Differentiation Formula

1.$\frac{d}{d x}\left(x^n\right)=n \cdot x^{n-1}$

2.$\frac{d}{d x}[c]=0$

3.$\frac{d}{d x}\left(e^x\right)=e^x$

4.$\frac{d}{d x}\left(a^x\right)=a^x \ln (a)$

5.$\frac{d}{d x}(\ln (x))=\frac{1}{x}$

6.$\frac{d}{d x}\left(\log _a(x)\right)=\frac{1}{x \ln (a)}$

7.$\frac{d}{d x}(\sin x)=\cos x$

8.$\frac{d}{d x}(\cos x)=-\sin x$

9.$\frac{d}{d x}(\tan x)=\sec ^2 x$

10.$\frac{d}{d x}(\cot x)=-\cosec ^2 x$

11.$\frac{d}{d x}(\sec x)=\sec x \tan x$

12.$\frac{d}{d x}(\cosec x)=-\cosec x \cot x$

Constant Multiple Rule

$\text { If } y=c f(x)=c U \text {, then }: \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{d(c U)}{d x}=c \frac{d U}{d x}$

Addition/Subtraction Rule

If U and V are functions of x and y is sum of functions U and V :

$y=U \pm V, \frac{d(U \pm V)}{d x}=\frac{d U}{d x} \pm \frac{d V}{d x}$

Product Rule

$\frac{d(U V)}{d x}=V \frac{d U}{d x}+U \frac{d V}{d x}$

Quotient Rule

$\frac{d\left(\frac{U}{V}\right)}{d x}=\frac{V \frac{d U}{d x}-U \frac{d V}{d x}}{V^2}$

Rules of Differentiation - Chain Rule

If $y = f(U)$

$\displaystyle \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{d f(U)}{d U} \times \frac{d U}{d x} ,$

Power Chain Rule

$\text { If } y=U^n \text { then } \frac{d y}{d x} \text { will be given by : }$

$\frac{d y}{d x}=n U^{(n-1)} \frac{d U}{d x}$

Application of Derivatives

Slope of a curve at a given point

$\mathrm{m}_{\text {inst }}=\tan \theta=\frac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{dx}}$

Function to First Derivative:

$y = f(x) \quad \xrightarrow{\text{Differentiation}} \quad \frac{dy}{dx}$

First Derivative to Second Derivative :

$\frac{dy}{dx} \quad \xrightarrow{\text{Differentiation}} \quad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$

Maxima

Condition for maxima are :

$\frac{d y}{d x}=0 \text { and } \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}<0$

Minima

Condition for minima are:

$\frac{d y}{d x}=0 \text { and } \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}>0$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Integration:

$\int \mathrm{f}(\mathrm{x}) \mathrm{dx}=\mathrm{F}(\mathrm{x})+\mathrm{c}$

Formulae of Integration for Algebraic function

1.$\int x^n d x=\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}+c$

2.$\int \frac{1}{x} d x=\ln x+c$

3.$\int \mathrm{kdx}=\mathrm{kx}+\mathrm{c}$

4.$\int \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{x}} \mathrm{dx}=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{x}}+\mathrm{c}$

5.$\int \sin x d x=-\cos x+c$

6.$\int \cos x d x=\sin x+c$

Definite Integration :

When a function is integrated between a lower limit and an upper limit, it is called a definite integral.

$\int_{\mathrm{a}}^{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{f}(\mathrm{x}) \mathrm{dx}=[\mathrm{F}(\mathrm{x})]_{\mathrm{a}}^{\mathrm{b}}=[\mathrm{F}(\mathrm{~b})-\mathrm{F}(\mathrm{a})]$

Average Value of Function

$<y>=\frac{\int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{\mathrm{x}_2} \mathrm{f}(\mathrm{x}) \mathrm{dx}}{\int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{\mathrm{x}_2} \mathrm{dx}}$

$<\mathrm{y}>=\frac{\text { area under } \mathrm{y}-\mathrm{x} \text { curve }}{\text { range of } \mathrm{x}(\mathrm{~b}-\mathrm{a})}$

Area under a curve and definite integration

$\int_a^b f(x) d x=\text { shaded area between curve and } x \text {-axis. }$

$\int_{\mathrm{a}}^{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{f}(\mathrm{x}) \mathrm{dx}=[\mathrm{F}(\mathrm{x})]_{\mathrm{a}}^{\mathrm{b}}=[\mathrm{F}(\mathrm{~b})-\mathrm{F}(\mathrm{a})]$

Applications of Integration – Analytical

There are many applications of integration such as :

(a) Displacement/Change in position  $\Delta \mathrm{x}=\mathrm{x}_2-\mathrm{x}_1$

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{v}=\frac{\mathrm{dx}}{\mathrm{dt}} \\ & \int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{\mathrm{x}_2} \mathrm{dx}=\int_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{\mathrm{t}_2} \mathrm{vdt} \end{aligned}$

$\text { (Change in position) } \quad \mathrm{x}_2-\mathrm{x}_1=\int_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{\mathrm{t}_2} \mathrm{vdt}$

(b) Change in velocity  $\Delta v=v_2-v_1$

$a=\frac{d v}{d t}$

$\int_{\mathrm{v}_1}^{\mathrm{v}_2} \mathrm{~d} v=\int_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{\mathrm{t}_2} \mathrm{adt}$

$\text { (Change in velocity) } \quad \mathrm{v}_2-\mathrm{v}_1=\int_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{\mathrm{t}_2} \text { adt }$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Quadratic Equation: An algebraic equation of second order (Highest power of the variable is equal to 2) is called a quadratic equation.

$a x^2+b x+c=0$

$\text { where } a \neq 0$

The general solution of the quadratic equation

$\mathrm{x}=\frac{-\mathrm{b} \pm \sqrt{\mathrm{D}}}{2 \mathrm{a}}$ , $\text { where } D=b^2-4 a c$

Condition for Real and Imaginary Roots

$\begin{aligned} &\text { For Real Roots }\\ &\begin{aligned} & D \geq 0 \\ & b^2-4 a c \geq 0 \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} &\text { For Imaginary Roots }\\ &\begin{aligned} & D<0 \\ & b^2-4 a c<0 \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$

Sum and Product of Roots

$\begin{aligned} &\text { Sum of the roots }\\ &\mathrm{x}_1+\mathrm{x}_2=-\frac{\mathrm{b}}{\mathrm{a}} \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} &\text { Product of the roots }\\ &\mathrm{x}_1 \mathrm{x}_2=\frac{\mathrm{c}}{\mathrm{a}} \end{aligned}$

Binomial Theorem: An algebraic expression containing two terms is called a binomial expression

$(1+x)^n=1+n x+\frac{n(n-1)}{2 \times 1} x^2+\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{3 \times 2 \times 1} x^2+\ldots \ldots$

Arithmetic Progression (AP)

General form: a, (a + d), (a + 2d), ……., [a + (n – 1) d]

Here First Term : a

Common Difference : d

$\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{th}} \text { Term : } \quad[\mathrm{a}+(\mathrm{n}-1) \mathrm{d}]$

$\begin{aligned} &\text { Sum of first } \mathrm{n} \text { terms: }\\ &\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{n}}=\frac{\mathrm{n}}{2}\left[1^{\text {st }} \text { term }+\mathrm{n}^{\text {th }} \text { term }\right] \Rightarrow \mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{n}}=\frac{\mathrm{n}}{2}[2 \mathrm{a}+(\mathrm{n}-1) \mathrm{d}] \end{aligned}$

Geometric Progression (GP)

$\text { a, ar, } \operatorname{ar}^2, \ldots \ldots \ldots \ldots \ldots \operatorname{ar}^{(n-1)}$

First Term : a

Common Ratio : r

$\mathrm{n}^{\text {th }} \text { Term: }$$\mathrm{ar}^{(\mathrm{n}-1)}$

$\begin{aligned} &\text { Sum of first } \mathrm{n} \text { terms : }\\ &S_n=\frac{a\left(1-r^n\right)}{(1-r)} \end{aligned}$

Sum of all the terms of an infinite GP $S_{\infty}=\frac{a}{(1-r)} ; \text { Only when }|r|<1 $

Formulae to Remember

blocks.text:
Addition of  vectors

1.Triangle law of addition of two vectors: If two vectors are represented by two sides of a triangle in same order then their sum or 'resultant vector' is given by the third side of the triangle taken in opposite order of the first two vectors.

$\vec{R} = \vec{A} + \vec{B}$

2. Parallelogram Law:  If two vectors are represented by two adjacent sides of a parallelogram which are directed away from their common point then their sum (i.e. resultant vector) is given by the diagonal of the parallelogram passing away through that common point.

$\overrightarrow{PQ} + \overrightarrow{PS} = \overrightarrow{PR}$

$\vec{R} = \vec{A} + \vec{B}$

Analytical Method

$|\mathbf{R}| = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + 2AB \cos \theta}$

$|\vec{A} + \vec{B}| = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + 2AB \cos \theta}$

$In~ ΔOPQ$

$\tan \alpha = \frac{QP}{OQ}$=$\frac{B \sin \theta}{A + B \cos \theta}$

$\tan \beta = \frac{A \sin \theta}{B + A \cos \theta}$

Special Cases:

(1) If two vectors are parallel : $\theta = 0^\circ$

$|\vec{R}|_{\text{max}} = A + B$

(2) If two vectors are anti-parallel: $\theta =180^\circ$

$|\vec{R}|_{\text{min}} = A - B$

(3) If two vectors are perpendicular: $\theta = 90^\circ$

$|\vec{R}| = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2}$

$\vec{R} = \left| \vec{A} + \vec{B} \right| = 2A \cos \left( \frac{\theta}{2} \right)$

Note: $A - B \leq |\vec{A} + \vec{B}| \leq A + B$

Properties of vector addition:

1. Vector addition is commutative :$\vec{A} + \vec{B} = \vec{B} + \vec{A}$

2.Vector addition is associative:  $\left( {\vec A + \vec B} \right) + \vec C = \left( {\vec B + \vec C} \right) + \vec A = \left( {\vec C + \vec A} \right) + \vec B$

3.If two vectors  $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}}
$ & $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{~B}}$ are of equal magnitude ,i.e $|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}}|=|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}|=\mathrm{a}$.

Then the magnitude of their vector addition: $\left| {\vec R} \right| = \left| {\vec A + \vec B} \right| = 2a\cos \left( {\frac{\theta }{2}} \right)$

Addition of more than two vectors (law of polygon): If some vectors are represented by sides of a polygon in same order, then their resultant vector is represented by the closing side of polygon in the opposite order.

$\vec{R} = \vec{A} + \vec{B} + \vec{C} + \vec{D}$

If n coplanar vectors of equal magnitude are at equal angular separation $(\frac{360^\circ}{n})$ then their resultant is always ZERO.

Subtraction of two vectors :

Let $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are two vectors. Their difference  $\vec{A} - \vec{B}$ can be treated as sum of the vector $\vec{A}$ and $({- \overrightarrow{B}})$.

$\vec{A} - \vec{B} = \vec{A} + (-\vec{B})$

$|\vec{A} - \vec{B}| = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 - 2AB \cos \theta}$

$\tan \alpha = \frac{B \sin \theta}{A - B \cos \theta}$

Properties of vector subtraction :

1.Vector subtraction does not follow commutative law

$\vec{A} - \vec{B} \neq \vec{B} - \vec{A}$

2.Vector subtraction does not follow associative law

$(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}}-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}})-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{C}} \neq (\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{C}})-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}}\neq (\overrightarrow{\mathrm{C}}-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}})-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}$

3.If two vectors are of  equal magnitude i.e $|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}}|=|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}|=\mathrm{a}$ then magnitude of their vector subtraction

$|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{s}}|=$$\left| \vec{A} - \vec{B} \right| = 2a \sin \left( \frac{\theta}{2} \right)$

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Resolution of Vectors: To break or split a vector in components is called resolution of vector. Any vector can be split in two or more than two components.

Note: Maximum number of components of a vector can be infinite.

Vector Resolution in A Plane (2D): If the angle between components is 90°, then they are known as perpendicular/orthogonal /rectangular components.

$A_x = \text{Component of } \vec{A} \text{ along the x-axis}$

$A_y = \text{Component of } \vec{A} \text{ along the y-axis}$

$A_x = A \cos \theta$

$A_y = A \sin \theta$

$\vec{A} = A_x \hat{i} + A_y \hat{j}$

$\vec{A} = A \cos \theta \, \hat{i} + A \sin \theta \, \hat{j}$

$|\vec{A}| = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2}$

$\tan \theta = \frac{A_y}{A_x}$

$\tan \phi = \frac{A_x}{A_y}$

Here  $\theta$ is angle between $\vec{A}$ and its x component Here $\phi$ is angle between $\vec{A}$ and its y component

Resolution of vectors in 3-D

If  $\vec{A}$ makes angle $\alpha$ with x- axis angle $\beta$with y- axis angle $\gamma$ with z- axis.

Component of $\vec{A}$ along x axis is $\mathbf{A}_{\mathbf{x}}$

Component of $\vec{A}$ along y- axis is $\mathbf{A}_{\mathbf{y}}$

Component of $\vec{A}$ along z- axis is $\mathbf{A}_{\mathbf{z}}$

$\cos \alpha=\frac{A_x}{A} \Rightarrow A_x=A \cos \alpha \quad ; \cos \beta=\frac{A_y}{A} \Rightarrow A_y=A \cos \beta \quad ; \cos \gamma=\frac{A_z}{A} \Rightarrow A_z=A \cos \gamma$$$

Here, $cos \alpha$, $\cos \beta$ and  $\cos \gamma$ are known as direction cosines of  $\vec{A}$

$\text { As, } A_x, A_y \text { and } A_z \text { are components of } \vec{A} $

$\vec{A}=A_x \hat{\imath}+A_y \hat{\jmath}+A_z \hat{k} \Rightarrow A=\sqrt{A_x^2+A_y^2+A_z^2}$

$\sin ^2 \alpha+\sin ^2 \beta+\sin ^2 \gamma=2$

$\cos ^2 \alpha+\cos ^2 \beta+\cos ^2 \gamma=1$

$\vec{A}=A_x \hat{\imath}+A_y \hat{\jmath}+A_z \hat{k} \Rightarrow \frac{\vec{A}}{A}=\frac{A_x}{A} \hat{\imath}+\frac{A_y}{A} \hat{\jmath}+\frac{A_z}{A} \hat{k} \Rightarrow \widehat{A}=\cos \alpha \hat{\imath}+\cos \beta \hat{\jmath}+\cos \gamma \hat{k}$

Multiplication of a Vector by Scalar:

1. Whenever a vector is multiplied by a positive number then the new vector has same direction but its magnitude changes depending on number.

2. Whenever a vector is multiplied by a negative number then the new vector has opposite direction and its magnitude changes depending on number.

blocks.title: Dot Product
blocks.text:
Scalar Product: The scalar product of two vectors $\vec{A}$ and$\vec{B}$ equals to the product of their magnitudes and the cosine of the angle $\theta$ between them.

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~B}}=|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}}||\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}| \cos \theta$

Range of dot product: $-{A B} \leq \overrightarrow{{A}} \cdot \overrightarrow{{B}} \leq {A B}$

Notes:

• Dot product of two perpendicular vectors is always zero

• If the dot product of two non-zero vectors is zero, then $\theta=90^{\circ}$

$\begin{aligned} & \vec{A} \cdot \vec{A}=A^2 \\ & \widehat{A} \cdot \widehat{A}=1 \end{aligned}$

$\hat{\mathrm{i}} \cdot \hat{\mathrm{i}}=\hat{\mathrm{j}} \cdot \hat{\mathrm{j}}=\hat{\mathrm{k}} \cdot \hat{\mathrm{k}}=1$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Vector product :The vector product or cross product of any two vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ denoted as $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}(\mathrm{read} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~A}} \text { cross } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}})$ is defined as  $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}=\mathrm{AB} \sin \theta \hat{\mathrm{n}}$

Here $\theta$ is the angle between the vectors and the direction  is given by the right-hand-thumb rule($\overrightarrow{\mathrm{n}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}$)

  • Vector product of two vectors is always a vector perpendicular to the plane containing the two vectors, i.e. orthogonal (perpendicular) to both the vectors $\vec{A}$ and  $\vec{B}$
• Vector product of two vectors is not commutative

Application of Cross Product

1. To Find Area of Geometrical Shape

a. $\text { Area of Triangle }=\frac{1}{2}|\vec{A} \times \vec{B}|$

b. Area of Parallelogram

$\text { Area of parallelogram }=|\vec{A} \times \vec{B}| \quad $

Case II: If $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$  are diagonals of parallelogram

$\text { Area of parallelogram }=\frac{1}{2}|\vec{A} \times \vec{B}|$

2.To Find Unit vector perpendicular to given plane

$\hat{\mathrm{n}}= \pm \frac{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}}{|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{~A}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}|}= \pm \frac{\widehat{\mathrm{A}} \times \widehat{\mathrm{B}}}{\sin \theta}$

3. To Check Coplanarity

$\text { If } \vec{A}, \vec{B} ~\& ~ \vec{C} \text { are three coplanar vectors then }\\ (\vec{A} \times \vec{B}) \cdot \vec{C}=0 \Rightarrow[\vec{A}, \vec{B}, \vec{C}]=0$
